This exercise is about testing the conditional convergence prediction of the Solow model. The data comes from the Penn World Tables (PWT). The PWT provide national income accounts converted to international prices for 189 countries/territories for some or all of the years 1950-2017. The European Union or the OECD provide more detailed real product estimates for their countries and the World Bank makes current price estimates for most PWT countries at the GDP level.

Go to the PWT website http://www.rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/ and familiarize yourself with the documentation and the variables in the database. You will end up using this database extensively for your paper. Go to the online data access tool https: //pwt-data-tool.streamlit.app/ or download Excel or Stata fles on https://www. rug.nl/ggdc/productivity/pwt/ and construct the following dataset:

• Go to "Thematic Select" and select the following 10 countries: Belgium, Canada, Switzerland, Germany, France, UK, Italy, Japan, Netherlands, US. • Download the expenditure-side real GDP at chained PPP's in 2017 US dollars, and the number of persons engaged for every available year for these countries. (You can export the results to.xlsx.) • Compute the real GDP per worker at chained PPP's by dividing the total GDP each year by the number of persons engaged in that year. • Compute the average growth rate of GDP per worker between 1950 and 2017 for each of the ten countries. • Reduce the dataset to a small dataset with 10 observations and 3 variables: – country names – average growth rate $g_{i}$ for every country from 1950 to 2017 – log GDP per labor in the year $1950, y_{1950,i}$ (measured in 2017 US dollars)

Use this dataset to produce a scatterplot with the average growth rate of GDP per labor on the y-axis and GDP per labor in 1950 on the x-axis. Comment on the results. In particular, to what extent can these results be reconciled with the Solow model? Would the scatterplot look different if we included a greater set of countries, say all the countries available in the PWT data set? Why or why not? (You don't need to redo the analysis for all the countries. You can refer to the lecture notes or the readings here.)

In Lecture Note 4 we introduced the idea of "poverty traps" and showed how to capture it in the Solow model. Skim through the paper by Kraay and McKenzie (2014, JEP) posted on Canvas. The authors criticize a number of mechanisms put forward in the literature on why poverty traps might occur. Focus on the first two of those ("saving-based" and "big push") and write one paragraph (or two) for each, first describing the specific mechanism that leads to poverty traps and then Kraay and McKenzie's critique. If you have any counterargument to Kraay and McKenzie's critique, briefy mention it.
